label: text
text: The French Chamber of Deputies has rejected the vote of confidence in M. Herriot, "The new Premier, who has placed the negotiation of his " short-lived Cabinet in the hands of the President."

label: text
text: In spite of the talk of dictatorships, revolutions, and evidences rising of an anti-American and in a lesser degree anti-British feeling among Parisians, authoritative French circles in London do not consider that sensational developments are likely in France. They believe that the Herriot Cabinet cannot last and that a Poincare combination is probable. The latter may politically be undesirable in Great Britain, but it is emphasised that the French Government has enough to do to stabilise the franc without going back on Locarno.

label: text
text: The excitement in the lobbies of the Chamber was more intense even than yesterday. A feature of the situation has been the tendency for further splitting of parties A meeting of the Radical-Socialists to-day formed an inter-party group to promote the idea of a Ministry of the National Union.

label: text
text: The Socialists have not yet decided to support M. Herriot. It is even suggested that the Government may be unable to appear in Parliament because it is unable to count on all the support of which it had been assured.—Reuter.

label: text
text: In a packed Chamber M. Herriot read the Ministerial declaration, stating that the Government immediately concentrated attention on the financial problem. Immense difficulties were looming ahead, and the Government would consider it necessary to meet these difficulties, even those most pressing, in close conjunction with Parliament. He added:—

label: text
text:
“France intends paying the debt she contracted in defence of liberty. We absolutely refuse to resort to any increase in the limit of our note circulation, and reserve to ourselves absolute independence. Our object is to stabilise the franc.”
The declaration had a very cold reception.—Reuter

label: text
text: An amplification of the Ministerial declaration says that the Government's programme is based on the conviction that the country ought to save itself with its own resources. France intends to pay the debts contracted for the defence of liberty to the extent and in the form in which she will be certain to be able to keep the undertakings she makes. Foreign securities held outside France by Frenchmen must be repatriated. The Government intends to prepare the final return of freedom of capital by a fresh offer of amnesty, the refusal of which will be punished by severe penalties. Taxation will be rearranged in a more equitable manner and expenditure will be reduced.—Reuter.

label: text
text:
The Chamber rejected the vote of confidence by 290 votes to 237—a majority of 53.
The vote was followed by a statement by M. De Monzie that 38 milliard francs, which was the maximum which the Banque de France could legally advance to the State, was exhausted within 60 millions.—Reuter.

label: text
text: After the vote all the Ministers walked out except M. De Monzie, who asked the Chamber to vote immediately the Bill authorising the Banque de France to use part of the Morgan credits to enable the State to meet its obligations.

label: text
text: The sitting was suspended whilst the Finance Committee discussed the Bill:

label: text
text: Huge crowds in front of the Chamber cheered and yelled when M. Herriot's collapse was announced

label: text
text: M. de Monzie subsequently announced that the figure of 60,000,-000 francs at the Treasury's credit balance had now increased to 150,000,000 francs though he did not explain how the increase had arisen.—Reuter

label: text
text: "We fought well", rearked M. Herriot late in the evening on the termination of his visit to the President to whom he handed the Cabinet's resignation. — Reuter.

label: text
text:
Public interest in the debate was unprecedented in the history of the Republic. Tremendous crowds outside the Palais Bourbon showed "Dissolution." They booed M. Herriot and burst into cheers whet the result of the division was announced.
"The Police were requisitioned to keep order, the atmosphere being one of feverish excitement."

label: text
text:
Before the Adjournment Mr. de Monzie asserted that if the Chamber did not pass the Bill dealing with the Morgan credits he personally would take the responsibility of authorising the bank to sell part of the loan in order to save the bank suspending payments on the Treasury's account even if he were afterward arraigned before the High Court.
M. Poincare is at present a

label: text
text: M. Poincare is at present a warm favourite for the Premier-ship.—Reuter.

label: text
text: At 1:30 this morning M. Poincare accepted the President's invitation to form a Cabinet.—Renter.

label: text
text:
M. Poincare's Government is most likely to be of the nature of an Emergency Committee' comprised of only half a dozen Ministers.
A night sitting of the Chamber adopted a Bill authorising the Finance Minister to arrange an agreement with the Banque de France under which the Minister will return to the Banque currencies held by the Treasury, also authorising an increase in the limit of the note issue by a sum corresponding with the sale of currencies which will be carried out.—Reuter.

label: text
text: French francs closed at 219½ and Belgian francs at 213½.—

label: text
text: Europe is naked and shivering in a barrel whilst Mr. Andrew Mellon (U.S. Secretary of the Treasury), costly wrapped in clothes consisting of war debt, settlements and bank notes, is blandly remarking: "You may keep the barrel" is the subject of a cartoon in the New York World, which, in an accompanying leader, says that Mr. Winaton Churchill's rebuke contained in his speech in the House of Commons on July 19 is humiliating and fundamentally unanswerable. It adds that Mr. Mellon "with the finesse of a while elephant," signed a public letter written probably by some bureaucrat in the Treasury, which was wrong in its facts and nauseating in its pretensions at generosity.

label: text
text: The World concludes that President Coolidge's debt policy is merely a timid evasion to satisfy Congress.

label: text
text: The Herald and Tribune takes the other side of the inter-Allied debt question, protesting that the transactions with the Allies were above board and carried no legal or moral pledge of cancellation. It declares that with Great Britain the refunded debt is a matter of sound national policy, whereby the restoration of the pound to parity greatly helped, and Great Britain's position as a great "commercial creditor nation is strengthened!—Reuter's Service.

label: paragraph_title
text:
Plunging in Francs.
Noy York. July

label: text
text: Remembering the debacle of the German mark speculators in Wall Street were uneasy this morning at the continued plunging in the franc although the latter soon rallied on strong buying support.

label: text
text: A cable from Paris that Frenchmen are eagerly changing francs into American securities was a further unsettling element and as a result the Stock Market, which has been strong for some weeks, became hesitant as traders adopted a watching attitude to see whether the new French administration was able to improve the situation. Reuter's American Service.

label: text
text:
New York, July 21.
In view of the fall in the fran
and the prominence given in the
Press to the war debt controversies,
the eyes of the American public
are focused on Europe, especially
France. Uneasiness is increasing in
regard to the outcome of France's
difficulties, whilst newspapers give
prominence to reports of anti-
America demonstrations in France
and anti-American feeling in Great
Britain.

label: text
text: The American Press so far has been remarkably moderate in tone sympathizing with Europe's difficulties, but the man in the street is of opinion that France does not want to pay.

label: text
text: The Treasury has issued a statement amounting to a flat contradiction of Mr. Winston Churchill's figures of British expenditure in the United States in war time. Some politicians accuse Mr. Mellon of excessive generosity in debt settlements, particularly the Italian debt.—Reuter.

label: text
text:
A sensational "rumour that" the Banque de France might be to feed to suspend payments to "morrow" on account of the note circulation having reached the legal maximum, caused a sharp break in the Stock Market. Toward the close scores of prices broke from two to eight points. The French franc lost half of its earlier gain of 20 points.
The rumour persisted the whole afternoon, being supported by faring head lines in some of the coming papers.

label: text
text: Finally a Press despatch from Paris explained that the report was due to a misinterpretation of M. De Monzie's announcement.—Router.

label: text
text: Frances opened to-day at 244 to the £.

label: text
text:

The France has improved, and is now 226½.

label: text
text: The police were summoned to settle a brawl in the Montmartre Cafe, consequent on foreign tourists' remarks regarding the franc, which were resented by the French customers.

label: text
text: A motor coach full of tourists, passing Montmartre, was hooted by the crowd, some of whom mounted the foot-board and molested the passengers.

label: text
text: A gendarme drew a revolver and kept back the crowd, while the couch put on full speed and drove off.

label: text
text: Three American revellers, seated on a bench in Montmartre, were surrounded by loafers, but were rescued by the police.

label: text
text: From the President downwards the most dismal prophecies us to the probable early downfall of the Herriot Government are forthcom-

label: text
text: The "Echo de Paris" declares that M. Doumergue recently said that M. Herriot would "do the best he can but as you are going to fall in any case, get it over as soon as possible. Summon Parliament on Wednesday, instead of Thursday, so I can gain a day, in which to settle the crisis. Get a new Government formed."

label: text
text: This may account for the decision reached by M. Herriot to test the position of Parliament today instead of to-morrow by asking for vote of confidence after submitting a Ministerial declaration. This is confined almost entirely to finance.

label: text
text: The newspaper forecast indicates the determination of M. De Monzie—about whom the false alarm circulated last night that he had resolved to resign as Finance Minister—to discard exaggerated tenderness for certain interests.

label: text
text: M. De Monzie, interviewed by "Lo Matin" says, "I am not a bogey man, and have no scheme for a capital levy. My plans would alarm nobody."—Router's Service.
